\chapter{Numbers 11–20 and Weather}
\label{ch:te-numbers-and-weather}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what the weather is doing in Telugu and count past ten up to twenty.}

Say \te{వాతావరణం} — a pure Sanskrit vāta + āvaraṇa, \textquotedblleft{}the covering of air\textquotedblright{} — and report the weather with \te{వర్షం} \te{పడుతోంది}, \textquotedblleft{}rain is falling.\textquotedblright{}
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\te{పదకొండు} — \te{ఇరవై}]{\te{పదకొండు}, \te{ఇరవై} — the same pattern, worn down one step further}

\label{lesson:TE-C20-padakondu-iravai}



\begin{quote}
You just watched Kannada's twenty split cleanly into \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{} + \textquotedblleft{}ten.\textquotedblright{} Telugu most likely comes from the exact same pattern — but centuries of extra erosion have worn it past the point of being visible today.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Telugu's teens echo \textbf{\te{పది}} (\emph{padi}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{ten}\textquotedblright{}) plus each digit — \textbf{\te{పదకొండు}} (\emph{padakoṇḍu}, 11), \textbf{\te{పన్నెండు}} (\emph{panneṇḍu}, 12), and onward through \textbf{\te{పందొమ్మిది}} (\emph{paṅdommidi}, 19) — the same \textquotedblleft{}digit + ten-echo\textquotedblright{} compounding you just saw in Kannada.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{ఇరవై}} (\emph{iravai}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{twenty}\textquotedblright{}) most likely continues the \textbf{same} pan-Dravidian pattern as Kannada's \emph{ippattu} — an old \textbf{*iru-}/\textbf{*renḍu} (\textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{}) root fused with an old \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} root — but here's the honest difference: centuries of sound change have worn \emph{iravai} down far enough that it no longer visibly splits into \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} on the surface, the way Kannada's \emph{ippattu} still does today. Telugu's own word for \textquotedblleft{}two,\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\te{రెండు}} (\emph{renḍu}), doesn't obviously show up inside \emph{iravai} anymore — treat this as the most likely comparative-Dravidian account rather than a transparent, easily re-derivable compound.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}padakoṇḍu, panneṇḍu\textquotedblright{} — 11, 12
  \item \textquotedblleft{}padi\textquotedblright{} — ten
  \item \textquotedblleft{}iravai\textquotedblright{} — twenty, most likely the same \textquotedblleft{}two-tens\textquotedblright{} idea as Kannada, just worn down further
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How are Telugu's teens built? (\textbf{\te{పది}} (ten) + a digit, compounded.) Does \textbf{\te{ఇరవై}} visibly split into \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{} + \textquotedblleft{}ten\textquotedblright{} today, the way Kannada's \emph{ippattu} does? (\textbf{No} — it most likely continues the same pan-Dravidian pattern, but erosion has worn away the visible split.) What's Telugu's word for \textquotedblleft{}two\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\te{రెండు}}, \emph{renḍu}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\te{వాతావరణం}]{\te{వాతావరణం} — \textquotedblleft{}the covering of air,\textquotedblright{} pure Sanskrit this time}

\label{lesson:TE-C20-vatavaranam}



\begin{quote}
Kannada's weather word mixed a Persian loan with a Sanskrit one. Telugu's is different again — a single, unmixed Sanskrit compound.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{వాతావరణం}} (\emph{vātāvaraṇam}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{weather, atmosphere}\textquotedblright{} — built entirely from Sanskrit:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\te{వాత}} (\emph{vāta}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{wind, air}\textquotedblright{}) — the same Sanskrit root behind \textbf{\te{వాయువు}} (\emph{vāyuvu}, \textquotedblleft{}wind,\textquotedblright{} and the wind-god Vāyu).
  \item \textbf{\te{ఆవరణ}} (\emph{āvaraṇa}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{covering, layer, enclosure}\textquotedblright{}).
\end{itemize}

So \emph{vātāvaraṇam} literally means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the covering of air}\textquotedblright{} — the layer of air surrounding everything, i.e., the atmosphere/weather. Unlike Kannada's \emph{havāmāna} (Persian \emph{hava} + Sanskrit \emph{māna}), \textbf{both} pieces here are Sanskrit — no Perso-Arabic loan involved at all.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \te{వర్షం} \te{పడుతోంది} — \textquotedblleft{}rain is falling\textquotedblright{}}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{వర్షం} \te{పడుతోంది}.} — \textquotedblleft{}It's raining.\textquotedblright{} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{rain is falling}.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{varṣaṁ paḍutōndi.}) — \textbf{\te{వర్షం}} (\emph{varṣaṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}rain\textquotedblright{}) is the same Sanskrit root, \emph{varṣā}, you'll see again in the Dravidian arc.
\end{quote}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vātāvaraṇam\textquotedblright{} — weather, \textquotedblleft{}the covering of air\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vāta\textquotedblright{} — wind/air, \textquotedblleft{}āvaraṇa\textquotedblright{} — covering
  \item \textquotedblleft{}varṣaṁ paḍutōndi\textquotedblright{} — it's raining, \textquotedblleft{}rain is falling\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two Sanskrit pieces of \textbf{\te{వాతావరణం}}, and what does the whole word literally mean? (\textbf{\te{వాత}}, \textquotedblleft{}air,\textquotedblright{} + \textbf{\te{ఆవరణ}}, \textquotedblleft{}covering\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the covering of air}.\textquotedblright{}) Is either piece a Persian/Arabic loan, like part of Kannada's word? (\textbf{No} — both pieces are Sanskrit.) What word does Telugu use for \textquotedblleft{}rain\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{\te{వర్షం}}, \emph{varṣaṁ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
